After severing his college connection here, Mr. Holland went into the ministry, where he was engaged for a time in a lucrative business, and by some economy and thrift which had characterized him throughout his college days, he amassed considerable wealth. He died at San Antonio; and left to the world, among other things, a noble family—his daughter, Mrs. Emma Jett, one of the best known women in San Antonio, still lives—and a host of former students another heritage, the memory of an honored, faithful, and sincere teacher.

In 1941 Lewis Holland in enlisted in Company D, Fourteenth Arkansas Confederate Infantry, and went with his command to Savoy. He surrendered. Afterward he came to Texas. He was a teacher in the Methodist Church, with which church he was connected for many years, and to which denomination he has devoted most of his life, interested in the interests of the Church and widely known as the Baptist Standard.

As more than half of his active life was passed by Reverend Holland in the service of his Church, it is appropriate to quote the obituary editorial of the Baptist Standard for August 24, 1888, the week in which Holland passed away:

The editor of the Standard is unable to express the deep sense of sorrow that he felt when the tidings of the death of our dear friend and co-laborer, Professor Holland, came to his ears. Dr. Hanks having acquired an interest in the Baptist, was then known as the Western Baptist. In 1905, the institution enlarged its service and became a paper to the Baptist Standard, and which was one of the founder of the paper which later evolved into the Baptist Standard. This is why so many of the readers of the Baptist Standard feel bereaved at the death of Professor Holland, for he was one of the very men who made the Baptist Standard what it is and has been for so many years.
